18.5 Licensing and market entry

18.5.1 The market-entry correction must join legal status to operational permission. As at the evidence cut-off, PVARA’s official licensing page accepts NOC applications and describes the full VASP licensing route as forthcoming.420 That public position should be replaced, when legally and operationally ready, by a status architecture that no customer, bank, court or overseas regulator can mistake.

18.5.1 Separate entity status from activity permission

18.5.1.1 A licence should identify the legal person, controlling owners, approved senior management, Pakistan establishment or responsible contact, permitted activities, customer classes, conditions, effective date and status. It should not operate as an undifferentiated permission to perform every Schedule I service. Each activity permission should be supported by demonstrated capital, governance, systems, staffing, outsourcing and wind-down capability.

18.5.1.2 The public register should use controlled statuses: NOC holder; transition applicant; application complete and under assessment; licensed with named permissions; licensed with restriction; suspended; surrender in progress; revoked; rejected; and exited. “Registered”, “approved” and “regulated” should not be used unless the underlying legal status justifies them. Historic entries should remain visible with dates so that a customer can determine the provider’s status when a transaction occurred.

18.5.2 Use a lawful transition matrix

18.5.2.1 PVARA should decide each inherited case through a published matrix rather than negotiate bespoke legal states. An existing NOC holder that files a complete and timely application may continue only within the section 70 bridge and applicable directions. A non-NOC existing provider must prove that it falls within the statutory class and meet the same completeness and protective floor; the existence of business before the Act is not itself an approval. A new entrant should not rely on section 70. An overseas provider targeting Pakistan should be classified under the statutory nexus and cross-border module rather than allowed to treat remote access as absence from the jurisdiction.

18.5.2.2 Where final Regulations are not in force when a statutory decision must be made, PVARA should identify which criteria arise directly from the Act and which cannot lawfully be improvised. The answer may be a narrow amendment or properly made interim instrument; it is not an unpublished scoring model. Applicants should receive a deficiency notice, reasonable opportunity to cure where law permits, and a reasoned determination. PVARA should publish service standards but avoid promising approval by a date irrespective of complexity.

18.5.3 Make fitness, ownership and governance continuing duties

18.5.3.1 Fit-and-proper assessment should apply to beneficial owners, controllers, directors, key executives and persons controlling critical wallets or systems. It should examine integrity, competence, financial soundness, conflicts, regulatory history and capacity relevant to the role. Foreign findings should be verified and weighed, not automatically imported. A refusal based on confidential intelligence still requires a lawful method of giving sufficient substance to answer the case.

18.5.3.2 Change of control, material outsourcing, new activity, key-person departure, serious incident and financial deterioration should trigger notification or prior approval according to risk. Nominee arrangements and token-based governance must not obscure control. The provider should maintain an ownership-and-control map showing legal rights, practical influence, privileged access, treasury authority and dependencies. The Authority should retain an intervention and wind-down plan for every material provider.

18.5.4 Calibrate prudential requirements to loss channels

18.5.4.1 Capital should not be a single number copied across unlike businesses. The methodology should identify fixed overhead, custody exposure, credit and counterparty risk, settlement exposure, market risk, operational risk, group concentration and wind-down cost. Client assets do not count as the provider’s capital. Insurance may mitigate a defined loss but should not replace governance or liquid resources.

18.5.4.2 A low-footprint adviser may justify a different requirement from a custodian, exchange, lender or leveraged-derivative platform, yet each must hold resources sufficient for orderly exit. Thresholds and calculations should be public, with a power to impose an evidenced add-on and a right to reasons and review. The proof is not merely a submitted return: PVARA must reconcile capital to audited accounts, wallet and bank evidence, liabilities, group transfers and stress results.

18.5.5 Control foreign reliance without automatic passporting

18.5.5.1 A foreign licence may reduce duplicated evidence where the home regime and supervisor can be verified. It should not automatically confer a Pakistan permission. PVARA must assess Pakistan nexus, local accountability, customer remedies, data and record access, asset location, insolvency consequences, supervisory cooperation and exit. Any equivalence or reliance determination should be published, scoped, time-limited and reviewable. Marketing into Pakistan should stop if the relied-on status lapses or effective cooperation fails.

18.5.5.2 Licensing completion requires a searchable register, consistent reasons, review notices, regulatory interfaces, assigned supervision, asset verification, incident escalation and an exercised exit. Licence volume alone proves little.

18.6 Financial perimeter, stablecoins and tokenised finance

18.6.1 The VAA does not repeal or subordinate the laws governing currency, banking, deposits, payment systems, foreign exchange, securities or derivatives. PVARA’s power to regulate a virtual-asset service therefore operates alongside SBP’s and SECP’s statutory mandates. The corrective programme should turn that coexistence into a visible decision system.421

18.6.1 Establish a joint perimeter mechanism

18.6.1.1 PVARA, SBP and SECP should adopt a protocol that routes a product to the competent decision-maker without transferring legal power. The intake should capture: legal issuer; holder’s claim; reserve and redemption; payment use; return or profit right; governance and control; custody; transfer and settlement; marketing; Pakistan nexus; and failure allocation. Each regulator then records whether its law applies, what permission is required and which unresolved point needs primary correction.

18.6.1.2 The resulting perimeter determination should name the lead regulator for each decision and list concurrent permissions. A PVARA VASP licence should not be described as SBP approval for payment or foreign-exchange activity, SECP approval of a security or fund, or validation of title to an underlying asset. Conversely, an SBP or SECP permission should not dispense with a VAA permission where a professional virtual-asset service is performed.

18.6.2 Regulate stablecoin functions, not the label

18.6.2.1 A token promoted as stable may embody a payment claim, stored value, debt, fund-like interest, contractual redemption promise, algorithmic mechanism or no enforceable stabilisation claim at all. The rulebook should classify these functions and reserve regulatory names for products meeting specified conditions. Before public distribution or admission, the responsible authority should identify the issuer, governing law, holder’s legal claim, reserve owner and custodian, permitted reserve assets, valuation, concentration, reconciliation, audit, redemption timing, fees, suspension conditions and insolvency treatment.422

18.6.2.2 Where the token is used for payment, settlement or conversion with Pakistani rupees, SBP’s payment, banking and foreign-exchange perimeter must be applied. PVARA may supervise the VASP and virtual-asset conduct; it cannot authorise the issue of currency or override foreign-exchange law. Where the token is a security, derivative or collective investment, SECP’s perimeter applies. A joint Financial-Referenced Token module should specify the hand-off, not invent a category outside the statutes.

18.6.2.3 Algorithmic stability requires a different control. The issuer or operator should disclose the mechanism, dependencies, governance keys, intervention authority, collateral if any, historical and simulated stress, oracle dependence, death spiral and wind-down. Distribution to retail customers should not proceed merely because a model held its target in benign conditions. The regulator should have authority to limit scale, require a sandbox, mandate warnings, order redemption or exit where promised, and halt misleading “stable” claims.

18.6.3 Build a lawful security-token and RWA bridge

18.6.3.1 Tokenisation does not itself transfer shares, debt, land, warehouse goods or beneficial ownership. The corrective package should require a legal-rights memorandum for any security token or real-world-asset token: the underlying right; issuer and obligor; registry or title system; perfection and priority; custodian or trustee; corporate and transfer restrictions; enforcement; insolvency; and reconciliation between the authoritative legal register and the token ledger.

18.6.3.2 PVARA and SECP should jointly publish classification examples and an intake route. Where another registrar or provincial property system is legally authoritative, the blockchain should be treated as evidence or an operating layer only to the extent that law recognises it. A smart contract cannot cure a defective conveyance. Pilot approval should be conditional on a tested correction process for lost keys, erroneous transfers, corporate actions, court orders and divergence between ledgers.

18.6.4 Use sandboxing as bounded evidence generation

18.6.4.1 The ART sandbox can test a product, control or interface under written conditions. It should not become a parallel licensing system or an exemption from another regulator’s law. Each cohort decision should state the legal basis, activities, customer and value limits, duration, safeguards, reporting, exit and the questions being tested. No public-money or retail scale should follow until the responsible authorities publish the evidence and decide the permanent route.

18.6.4.2 Proof requires a determination register and resolved test cases for a fiat-referenced token, tokenised share and property claim, payment wallet, lending protocol, leveraged token and mining service, each naming the authority, permissions, customer claim, safeguards and remedy.

18.7 Customer assets, market integrity and failure management

18.7.1 The customer-protection programme must make section 24 real at the point of failure. Disclosure is necessary, but it cannot substitute for legal segregation, control evidence, reconciliation and return. The central question is whether a customer can recover the correct asset, or legally determined equivalent, when a provider, bank, custodian, sub-custodian, protocol or key controller fails.423

18.7.1 Implement the safeguarding chain

18.7.1.1 Final Regulations should require a customer-asset architecture approved for each custodial activity. It should identify wallets and bank accounts; legal and beneficial ownership; persons capable of initiating, approving and broadcasting a transfer; hot, warm and cold controls; key generation, storage, backup, rotation and recovery; sub-custodians; settlement windows; and the data reconciling each customer entitlement to assets on-chain and off-chain.

18.7.1.2 Reconciliation should occur at a frequency matched to risk and after material events. Differences require categorisation, investigation, customer-protective funding where appropriate and notification above defined thresholds. A proof-of-reserves publication, if permitted, should not be described as proof of solvency: it may omit liabilities, borrowed assets, encumbrances, off-chain positions and control risk. Independent assurance should examine both assets and liabilities, ownership, control and the procedure used.

18.7.1.3 Customer terms should state whether assets are held in individual or omnibus form, whether sub-custody is used, governing law, forks and airdrops, staking or lending, fees, insurance, error correction, death or incapacity, complaints and insolvency treatment. Any reuse must be separately elected and recorded. A general platform consent should not convert safeguarded custody into unsecured lending.

18.7.2 Build an executable failure plan

18.7.2.1 Each custodian, exchange and lender should maintain a recovery and wind-down plan. It should map critical staff, keys, vendors, banks, nodes, data, customer communications and asset-transfer capacity; identify triggers; and estimate resources for reconciliation and return. PVARA should be able to require a solvent wind-down before insolvency, appoint or seek appointment of an appropriate administrator where authorised, and coordinate with company courts and liquidators.

18.7.2.2 The plan should be exercised through a failure simulation. A provider must demonstrate that an alternate authorised group can reconstruct entitlements, secure keys, stop unauthorised transfers, communicate with customers, honour lawful freezes and return assets. The exercise should include a shortfall and a disputed claim. The result, deficiencies and remediation date should form part of supervisory evidence.

18.7.3 Create a complete market-integrity rulebook

18.7.3.1 The Act’s market-abuse and disclosure provisions require detailed definitions, evidentiary rules and surveillance expectations. Regulations should address wash trading, matched orders, spoofing, layering, ramping, marking, pump-and-dump conduct, misuse of confidential information, front running, manipulative token supply or oracle inputs, misleading liquidity, undisclosed paid promotion and conflicts in listing or proprietary trading.

18.7.3.2 Operators should maintain order, trade, wallet, communication, listing and beneficial-control records capable of reconstructing conduct across on-chain and off-chain venues. Surveillance should combine rules and human review, document model changes and prevent a provider from treating every anomaly as guilt. Referral criteria should identify when PVARA, SECP, FMU, FIA/NCCIA or another competent body becomes responsible. Parallel interest does not authorise unrestricted data circulation.

18.7.4 Integrate complaints, compensation and remedy

18.7.4.1 Every licensed provider should operate a time-bound complaint process with acknowledgement, investigation, reasons, correction and escalation. PVARA should publish aggregate categories and outcomes, not merely accept portal submissions. The official grievance portal is useful administrative access, but it does not itself prove statutory adjudication, compensation authority or an operational Tribunal.424

18.7.4.2 The primary and delegated package should identify available remedies: correction of records, return of assets, reversal where legally and technically possible, compensation, fee refund, contract remedy, restitution, administrative direction, sanction and access to court. A compensation or fidelity arrangement should be adopted only after defining funding, coverage, exclusions, governance and relationship with insolvency. It must not socialise ordinary investment losses or imply State guarantee.

18.8 AML/CFT, Travel Rule, sanctions, data and cyber resilience

18.8.1 Financial-integrity and technology controls should be designed as one lawful operating chain. A VASP cannot conduct CDD, screen sanctions, monitor transactions, transmit Travel Rule data, report suspicion, preserve evidence and respond to an incident if identities, accounts, wallets, transfers and access logs cannot be linked reliably. Equally, the existence of powerful data does not authorise unrestricted collection or sharing.425

18.8.1 Complete the AML/CFT legal allocation

18.8.1.1 The Federal Government should verify and publish the operative AMLA Schedule IV or other lawful designation connecting PVARA and covered virtual-asset reporting entities to the statutory supervisory architecture. PVARA, FMU and the relevant AML authorities should then issue an allocation protocol covering registration, risk assessment, inspection, enforcement referral, suspicious transaction reporting, sanctions, confidentiality, feedback and protected information. The protocol should track legal powers; it should not make FMU an ordinary data service or give PVARA access to protected material without authority.

18.8.1.2 PVARA should publish a sectoral risk assessment distinguishing exchange, transfer, custody, broking, lending, issuance, mining-related activity, DeFi interfaces, privacy-enhancing technology and cross-border corridors. Regulatory requirements and supervisory frequency should follow the evidence. Small size is not automatically low risk; high transaction value is not the only indicator.

18.8.2 Operationalise the Travel Rule

18.8.2.1 A binding standard should define covered transfers, originator and beneficiary information, verification, message timing, counterparty-VASP due diligence, secure transmission, missing or inconsistent data, rejected or suspended transfers, record retention and error correction. It should be technology-neutral and interoperable. The standard must also specify the risk-based process for self-hosted addresses: ownership or control evidence where proportionate, purpose and counterparty risk, sanctions screening, transaction monitoring, enhanced due diligence and refusal criteria. It should not impose a categorical ban without legislative authority and evidence.426

18.8.2.2 Implementation proof requires end-to-end tests between providers and across borders. The test set should include a normal transfer, missing fields, name mismatch, sanctioned party, high-risk corridor, self-hosted address, technical outage, corrected record and lawful information request. Supervisors should measure completeness, accuracy, latency, false positives, disposition and protected-data access—not count installed software.

18.8.3 Integrate targeted financial sanctions

18.8.3.1 The rulebook should require current sanctions data, customer and beneficial-owner screening, wallet and transaction analytics appropriate to risk, escalation, freezing or rejection where law requires, reporting, controlled release and false-positive correction. It should identify the legal instrument that creates the obligation and the authority capable of directing action. A commercial risk score is evidence for assessment, not legal proof that a person is designated.

18.8.3.2 Providers and PVARA should maintain an auditable chain from the applicable designation through match logic, human decision, action, notice where permitted, report and review. Where secrecy is lawfully required, the system should still preserve a record for independent oversight and eventual challenge.

18.8.4 Enact and bridge data protection law

18.8.4.1 Pakistan needs comprehensive primary data-protection legislation establishing lawful processing, rights, controller and processor duties, sensitive-data safeguards, cross-border transfer rules, independent oversight, enforcement and remedies. Until that is enacted, PVARA should use the VAA, PECA, sectoral confidentiality duties, contract, constitutional rights and lawful Regulation powers to impose a bounded Virtual Asset Data Code without pretending that subordinate rules constitute a general national data law.427

18.8.4.2 The Code should require purpose specification, minimisation, accuracy, retention, access control, encryption, logging, processor governance, breach response, customer access and correction, and rules for regulatory disclosure. It should separate onboarding data, transaction monitoring, Travel Rule messages, biometric material, wallet analytics, complaints and enforcement evidence. Cross-border outsourcing should be conditional on legal access, security, deletion and regulator cooperation, not localisation rhetoric alone.

18.8.5 Establish operational-resilience and incident rules

18.8.5.1 PVARA should define critical services and impact tolerances, not merely recovery-time promises. Providers should map assets, keys, systems, people, vendors, cloud regions, banks, nodes, oracles and data flows; conduct threat-led tests proportionate to risk; manage vulnerabilities and changes; and maintain secure recovery. Material incidents should be classified by customer harm, asset loss, service disruption, data compromise, integrity failure and cross-sector effect.

18.8.5.2 The reporting standard should provide an immediate alert for critical incidents, a structured initial report, updates and a root-cause and remediation report. Timing should begin when the provider reasonably determines the classification, with controls against deliberate delay. PVARA should operate a 24-hour intake and coordinate with the competent cybercrime, data, financial and security bodies under a lawful protocol. Customer notice should be prompt unless a legally authorised delay is necessary to contain harm or protect an investigation.

18.8.5.3 Completion is demonstrated by exercises: compromised signing key; cloud-region outage; corrupted entitlement ledger; oracle manipulation; ransomware; insider exfiltration; and failure of the Travel Rule vendor. The exercise should test authority, decisions, evidence custody, customer communication, asset security, alternate processing and recovery—not only technical restoration.

18.9 Tax, reporting and federal–provincial coordination

18.9.1 Tax reform must begin with constitutional and charging discipline. The VAA’s tax-compliance clause does not classify an asset, create a charge, determine source, set valuation or impose withholding. Those consequences must arise under valid federal or provincial fiscal law.428

18.9.1 Enact a federal tax taxonomy through fiscal law

18.9.1.1 FBR should publish, and where necessary seek legislation for, a coherent event-based framework. It should address acquisition, disposal, exchange, payment, mining rewards, staking or validation rewards, airdrops, forks, lending yield, liquidity provision, derivatives, token issuance, employee compensation, gifts, inheritance, theft, loss and migration between personal wallets. For each event it should identify the taxpayer, head of income or gain, recognition time, basis, valuation source, deductible cost, loss treatment, records and withholding or reporting obligation.

18.9.1.2 The framework should distinguish accounting from tax and personal investment from business activity without relying on token labels. Valuation rules need a hierarchy for exchange-traded, thinly traded, non-convertible and related-party assets, with methods for absent or manipulated prices. Correcting section 66’s title is part of textual hygiene; it is not the tax reform.

18.9.1.3 Domestic reporting should precede any promise of automatic international exchange. FBR should define reporting entities, reportable users and assets, due diligence, data fields, correction, retention, confidentiality, enforcement and taxpayer challenge in tax law. The OECD Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework may inform design, but it does not apply itself in Pakistan. Treaty authority, domestic legislation, systems, security and an activated exchange relationship must exist before data is sent.

18.9.2 Resolve provincial services-tax treatment cooperatively

18.9.2.1 Virtual-asset services may engage provincial sales taxes on services while other fiscal consequences remain federal. The Federation and provinces should use the constitutional coordination machinery and revenue-authority cooperation to publish a common service map: exchange, brokerage, advisory, custody, management, transfer, lending facilitation, issuance services, mining pools and technology supply. The map should identify place-of-supply, business and customer location, inter-provincial service, input treatment, registration, invoicing and audit coordination.429

18.9.2.2 Harmonisation should not mean an executive transfer of taxing power. Each legislature or authorised revenue body must make the necessary rule within its competence. A common return or portal can reduce duplication only if its legal basis, data custody, assessment responsibility, payment allocation and appeal routes are clear. The implementation test is a set of transactions assessed consistently by FBR and each participating provincial authority, with no double collection and no unreviewable gap.

18.9.3 Connect mining to electricity and environmental law

18.9.3.1 PVARA licensing of a mining-related virtual-asset service does not allocate electricity, approve a connection, set a tariff or grant environmental permission. The responsible energy and provincial bodies should define categories, load data, connection studies, tariff treatment, curtailment, metering, grid impact, renewable claims, emissions and environmental screening. A mining permission should be conditional on the resulting approvals, not presented as their substitute.

18.9.3.2 Any public allocation of surplus power should be supported by independently verifiable system data, opportunity-cost analysis, fiscal approval, procurement or allocation authority, and a termination rule if the factual premise changes. Pilot results should disclose energy used, interruptions, public revenue and cost, environmental conditions, employment and enforcement—not projected token value alone.

18.10 Institutional responsibility, the Tribunal and customer redress

18.10.1 The reform programme needs a named owner for every decision and an escalation route for every blocked dependency. The VAA Board’s multi-agency composition assists coordination, but the Board is not a device for exercising the statutory powers of its members’ institutions. Each participating body should sign an institutional responsibility protocol that identifies the legal source, decision owner, required contributors, protected-information limits, service standard, record, escalation and review route.430

18.10.1 Build the responsibility protocol

18.10.1.1 The protocol should be supported by three schedules. A decision schedule lists recurring cases and the owner: licence, fiat-referenced token, tokenised security, suspicious transaction, customer-asset shortfall, cyber incident, tax information request, mining connection and cross-border provider. An information schedule identifies the exact fields that may be shared, legal basis, purpose, recipient, access, retention and onward-disclosure rule. An incident schedule establishes 24-hour contacts, severity, lead agency, preservation duties, customer communication and after-action review.

18.10.1.2 For each scheduled process, the institutions should conduct a tabletop and a live interface test. A memorandum signed but never exercised is not implementation proof. Failures should be assigned, dated and retested. Where an institution lacks staff, technology or legal authority, the dependency should be reported to the programme board rather than concealed by assigning the duty to a regulated entity.

18.10.1.3 The programme board should also test behaviour created by the implementation design: whether a referral is treated as delay, whether one agency's performance target pushes unresolved risk to another, whether shared work has an agreed evidential record and whether officers can escalate a legal disagreement without informal personal negotiation. The response is a transparent owner-and-escalation system with joint exercises and published service commitments, not an unsupported attribution of motive, ego or resistance.

18.10.2 Make the Tribunal an institution, not a statutory noun

18.10.2.1 The Tribunal requires a constitutionally defensible primary route and an operational package. That package includes appointment and removal safeguards; qualifications and conflicts; administrative and financial independence; registry and seal; filing and service; case allocation; record transmission; urgent and interim applications; condonation; hearings and evidence; publication and anonymisation; enforcement of orders; costs; further appeal or reference; and transition for pending matters.431

18.10.2.2 Before live reliance, the registry should process a synthetic case from an adverse PVARA decision through filing, service, record production, interim relief, hearing, signed order and onward review. The test should reveal whether a customer or small business can use the route without bespoke access. Accessibility requires clear forms, electronic and assisted filing, reasonable fees, language support where needed, disability access and protection of confidential material. Publication should enable legal learning without exposing keys, personal data or suspicious-transaction information.

18.10.3 Connect administrative redress to legal remedy

18.10.3.1 PVARA’s complaint channel should triage: provider complaint; supervisory intelligence; urgent asset or cyber event; alleged crime; tax or payment issue; and appealable PVARA decision. The customer should be told which route applies and what the portal cannot decide. Complaints about a provider should ordinarily go first to the provider unless urgency, conflict or futility justifies direct escalation. Complaints about PVARA require a structurally separate handling route and must preserve statutory and constitutional remedies.

18.10.3.2 The Authority should publish quarterly data on receipt, subject, provider response, time, outcome, systemic finding, referrals and outstanding age, with lawful privacy protection. It should identify repeated causes and use them in supervision. A high closure rate is not success if cases are administratively closed without correction or remedy.

18.10.4 Resource and hold institutions accountable

18.10.4.1 The capacity plan should cover legal drafting, authorisation, prudential and custody analysis, surveillance, AML/CFT, cyber, data, enforcement, economics, tax and records. It should identify build, train, second, procure and shared-service choices, with conflict and vendor-dependence controls.

18.10.4.2 PVARA’s annual plan should connect resources to application quality, risk-based supervision, asset exceptions, incidents, AML remediation, complaints, enforcement, appeals and unresolved interagency decisions. Licence count, volume and investment are context, not proof of regulatory success.

18.11 National strategy and National Digital Masterplan alignment

18.11.1 The digital-asset programme should sit in a lawful sectoral plan approved and monitored through the Digital Nation Pakistan Act 2025. That Act gives the National Digital Commission, Pakistan Digital Authority and National Digital Masterplan distinct roles and requires the PDA’s work on virtual assets and emerging technologies to avoid overlap with other regulatory mandates and conflict with existing law.432 The Masterplan is therefore the place to integrate cross-government dependencies; it is not authority for PDA to license or supervise VASPs.

18.11.1 Use a finance-sector implementation plan

18.11.1.1 The responsible federal Division should prepare a digital-assets sectoral implementation plan for Commission approval and Masterplan alignment. The plan should identify statutory outcomes, reform modules, owners, dependencies, resources, procurement, common infrastructure, indicators, risks, public reporting and review. PVARA, SBP, SECP, FMU, FBR, Law Division, relevant investigation bodies, provinces and the PDA should contribute within their mandates.

18.11.1.2 Each proposed national initiative should pass the twelve constitutional planning tests developed in Chapter 6: source of authority; lawful institution; federal–provincial competence; rights; public finance; procurement; data; cyber; regulatory perimeter; remedies; evidence; and revision. A label such as “national wallet”, “tokenised government asset”, “strategic reserve” or “mining hub” supplies none of those answers.

18.11.2 Separate regulatory foundations from market initiatives

18.11.2.1 The plan should contain two portfolios. The regulatory-foundation portfolio covers the amendment Bill, Rules, final Regulations, appointments, Tribunal, registers, interfaces, standards, capacity and tests. The market and public-use portfolio covers sandbox projects, tokenisation, payments, mining, investment promotion or public-sector uses. No initiative in the second portfolio should pass its scale gate until the applicable first-portfolio dependencies are complete.

18.11.2.2 For public-sector tokenisation or wallet use, the sponsoring institution must identify the legal asset, public-money flow, custodian, procurement, accounting, audit, cybersecurity, data, customer or citizen remedy, failure allocation and exit. A pilot should cap exposure and preserve an off-chain authoritative record where law requires. The State should not use a sandbox to avoid fiscal, procurement or constitutional control.

18.11.3 Align indicators with public outcomes

18.11.3.1 National reporting should distinguish inputs, outputs, operational outcomes and public outcomes. Staff hired and regulations issued are inputs and outputs. Accurate status, secure customer assets, reduced unresolved complaints, effective detection, predictable decisions, service recovery and lawful tax reporting are operational outcomes. Financial inclusion, investment quality, innovation, lower cross-border friction and reduced illicit finance are public outcomes that require evidence and counterfactual care.

18.11.3.2 The plan should publish baselines, definitions, source systems, frequency, owner and limitations. Commercial market estimates and chain-analytics outputs should be labelled as estimates. Regulatory data should not be repurposed for publicity without legal basis and quality review. The Commission’s monitoring record should disclose delayed dependencies and corrective decisions rather than convert every indicator into a success narrative.

18.11.3.3 At the evidence cut-off, official federal reporting described National Digital Masterplan consultations and implementation-roadmap work as ongoing. That supports active alignment work, not an inference that a final Commission-approved sector plan already exists.433 Chapter 18 therefore recommends the legal home and approval route; it does not invent approval.

18.12 Implementation sequence, dependencies and proof

18.12.1 The programme has three horizons from an adopted start date: Now: legality and continuity; Next: operational completion; and Then: evaluated scale and consolidation. These are planning bands, not section 70 rules or promises about parliamentary time. Movement depends on evidence gates.

18.12.1 Horizon I — Now: legality and continuity

18.12.1.1 The immediate horizon should complete the transition determination, authenticate governance and delegations, publish the instruments register, verify the Tribunal and investigation routes, finalise the section 74 continuity matrix, and establish the programme board and issue log. Government should settle drafting instructions for the targeted amendment Bill and Federal Rules. PVARA should dispose of consultation comments, publish its legal-authority concordance and identify which final regulatory modules can lawfully commence under the enacted Act.

18.12.1.2 Concurrently, the perimeter intake, AML allocation, tax taxonomy, provincial-tax and mining workstreams should begin. Existing customer-asset, AML/CFT, disclosure, records and incident duties remain applicable to the extent grounded in current law and valid instruments.

18.12.1.3 Horizon I requires authorised decision-makers, public status, a completeness method, an accurate appeal notice, protected incident contact and approved dependency report. A meeting is not completion.

18.12.2 Horizon II — Next: operational completion

18.12.2.1 Once the legal foundations are secure, Parliament and Government should progress the amendment Bill and Federal Rules through their lawful processes. PVARA should make the final Regulations, standards, forms and staged commencement package. Institutions should staff and test authorisation, supervision, customer-asset, market-surveillance, AML, cyber, enforcement, complaints and Tribunal workflows. Joint bodies should decide the model perimeter cases and publish permissible portions.

18.12.2.2 Every transition applicant should receive an evidenced status and continuity plan. Permission-based licensing and first-cycle supervision should test assets, key control, AML/Travel Rule operations, incidents, resources and wind-down, followed by remediation or lawful restriction.

18.12.2.3 Horizon II requires an accessible consistent rulebook, tested portals and schemas, a Tribunal test case, reasoned cross-regulator referrals, reconstructable customer assets and a candid first implementation report.

18.12.3 Horizon III — Then: evaluated scale and consolidation

18.12.3.1 Only after reliable operating evidence should the State expand sandboxes, rely on selected foreign evidence or scale public-use, mining and tokenisation initiatives. Incident, complaint, concentration, loss, AML, fiscal and performance data should control expansion; failing products remain capped, restricted or prohibited.

18.12.3.2 Government should commission an independent twelve-month implementation review measured from full operational commencement, not merely from the Act’s enactment. The review should examine legality, institutional independence, perimeter disputes, licensing quality, customer-asset failures, financial crime outcomes, data and cyber incidents, tax administration, remedies, costs, competition and innovation. Parliament should receive the report and the responsible institutions’ response. A later statutory review can determine whether a consolidated Act, further amendment or accepted residual risk is justified.

18.13.2 Table 18.5 places every missing-instrument identifier G-01–G-25 beside the audit item that controls its disposition. It also reconciles the workbook’s 24 issues: I-01–I-08 and I-10 map principally to the perimeter, issuer, customer-property, Tribunal, public-finance, Digital Nation and continuity items; I-09 and I-23 to blocking, coercive process, evidence and data; I-11–I-14 to AML, Travel Rule and tax; I-15 to market abuse and algorithmic tokens; I-16–I-18 to mining, environment, federalism and consumer redress; I-19, I-20 and I-24 to governance, the PCC and the instruments register; and I-21–I-22 to cross-border offerings and Shariah claims.435 Appearance in a Bill, draft or protocol does not close an item. Closure requires the stated proof.

18.13.3 Some residual risks may be accepted, monitored or studied where law is valid, safeguards operate and reasons are recorded. Unresolved authority, customer ownership, coercive process, tax, institutional validity and remedy remain legality gates. Scale should follow operating evidence, not innovation vocabulary.

Chapter 18 — Roadmap for Reform: The Corrective Package

Evidence cut-off. Legal and institutional status in this chapter was checked to 16 August 2026. Planning horizons are programme bands, not legal deadlines. Proposals remain subject to the Constitution, governing law, approval and publication requirements.

18.1 Bottom line and design principles

Pakistan does not need another declaration that digital assets matter. It needs a controlled conversion of enacted law into an operable legal order. The Virtual Assets Act 2026 (VAA) has already supplied a federal regulator, a functional service perimeter, licensing and issuer modules, customer-asset duties, preventive and supervisory powers, offences, an appellate design and delegated-law powers. The preceding chapters nevertheless show that enactment and operability are not the same thing. A statute can be in force while the entry route is transitional, the final rulebook remains incomplete, a cross-regulator boundary is unresolved, an institution has not been authenticated, or a remedy cannot yet be exercised predictably.412

The corrective package therefore begins from law already enacted. It does not treat the field as a clean slate, reproduce the Act in subordinate legislation or replace specialised regulators with a digital-asset super-regulator. It also does not ask regulated businesses to cure defects that belong to the State. A VASP can file a complete application, segregate customer assets and implement controls. It cannot appoint the Authority’s Board, establish a Tribunal, correct a statutory cross-reference, create a tax charge, allocate federal and provincial competence, or convert draft regulations into law. Those tasks must remain with the institutions legally empowered to perform them.

Eight principles govern the programme.

1. Legality before scale. No market-expansion target, public-wallet programme, mining allocation or tokenisation initiative should outrun the legal authority, customer protection, fiscal control and review mechanism applicable to it.

2. Instrument discipline. Parliament should decide essential policy, jurisdiction, coercive power, liability, tax and remedy. Federal Rules and PVARA Regulations should operationalise authority already conferred. Standards may specify testable technical requirements. Guidance may explain but must not create a disguised offence, licence condition or tax burden.

3. Function before label. The perimeter should turn on the legal and economic function actually performed, including control of assets, order execution, settlement, issuance, payment, investment intermediation and governance—not on names such as “utility token”, “protocol”, “DAO” or “decentralised”.

4. One decision, visible contributors. Where several regulators participate, one lawful decision-owner must be identifiable. Consultation does not transfer statutory power, and board membership does not merge mandates.

5. Transition without legal fiction. Continuity should protect customers and enable orderly applications. It should not imply that an NOC is a full licence, that a pending application is approved, or that a saved instrument is automatically valid for every Act-era purpose.

6. Proof, not promulgation alone. A Gazette notification is necessary where law requires it; it is not evidence that the regulated interface works. Completion requires authenticated instruments, named owners, working forms and data channels, trained decision-makers, tested remedies and published performance evidence.

7. Proportionality with a hard protective floor. Requirements may vary with activity, scale and risk, but segregation, governance, fitness, financial crime controls, truthful disclosure, operational resilience, reasons and access to review are not optional.

8. Revision by evidence. The regime should record incidents, supervisory findings, complaints, appeal outcomes, market concentration and implementation failures, and use them to revise subordinate instruments without concealing the version history.

Figure 18.1 — Corrective reform architecture

```mermaid

flowchart TD

A["Constitution and primary legislation"] --> B["Correct statutory defects and confer essential authority"]

B --> C["Federal Rules and PVARA Regulations"]

C --> D["Cross-regulator determinations and protocols"]

D --> E["Forms, registers, schemas, supervisory procedures and guidance"]

E --> F["Licensing, supervision, enforcement and redress in operation"]

F --> G["Published implementation evidence and independent review"]

G --> H["Retain, amend, coordinate, study, monitor or accept residual risk"]

H --> B

```

This hierarchy is also a sequencing rule. An administrative form cannot cure missing statutory authority. A memorandum cannot decide a legal perimeter entrusted to Parliament or another regulator. A technical standard cannot impose a penalty not authorised by the Act. Conversely, Parliament need not hard-code every cryptographic control or data field. The reform succeeds when each question is placed at the lowest level that can lawfully and durably answer it, while every higher-order safeguard remains intact.413

18.2 Immediate legal-validity corrections

The immediate programme is narrower than wholesale legislative redesign. Its purpose is to prevent the transition from producing avoidable illegality or uncertainty while the fuller package is prepared. Five corrections require priority.

18.2.1 Publish the transition position

Section 70 gives an existing provider a six-month bridge only if it submits a complete licence application within the statutory period and complies with interim directions and core obligations. Section 74 saves specified pre-Act matters, while section 73 permits removal of difficulties for six months but not an order inconsistent with the Act. These provisions should not be collapsed into a general amnesty.414 The exact terminal day should be confirmed by reasoned legal determination and officially published; this treatise does not manufacture certainty between 4 and 5 September 2026. The transition notice should state:

  • the class of provider capable of relying on section 70 and the evidence of existing activity;
  • what makes an application “complete”, how deficiencies are notified and whether a cured filing retains its original date;
  • the status of NOC holders, non-holders and applicants at each stage;
  • the obligations that apply during the bridge, including safeguarding, AML/CFT, disclosure, incident reporting and cooperation;
  • the consequences of rejection, withdrawal, incompleteness or expiry; and
  • customer-protection, transfer and wind-down requirements where authority to continue ends.

The notice must distinguish law from assistance. A checklist cannot extend the statutory period, and an NOC or pending application cannot be described as a licence. If the enacted transition cannot safely be completed, Parliament—not guidance—must alter it.

18.2.2 Authenticate appointments, delegations and decision authority

Before a body exercises coercive or determinative power, the public record should identify the lawful office-holder, appointment instrument, commencement date, term, vacancy status, delegation and any recusal. The Authority should publish a consolidated governance page linking the Board constitution, chairperson and member notifications, authorised committees, delegations under section 10, and the officers empowered to issue notices, decide applications, inspect, freeze, sanction or defend proceedings.415 Sensitive personal material need not be exposed. Legal authority must be.

Delegation instruments should identify the source power, delegate, subject, conditions, duration and retained powers, and preserve non-delegable functions. Proof requires a public delegation register cross-checked against protected signature and access controls.

18.2.3 Establish or authenticate the review route

The Act’s Tribunal and direct appellate route raise the constitutional and procedural concerns analysed in Chapter 16. The immediate response cannot wait for the first contested freeze or licence refusal. Government should publish the legal instruments establishing the Appellate Tribunal, appointments and terms, seat and filing channel, registry, procedural rules, fee and service arrangements, interim-relief jurisdiction, case-allocation method and route for further review—or state candidly which elements remain unavailable.416

Pending primary correction, every PVARA adverse decision should contain reasons, the legal source of power, the material relied on, the effective date, the available internal reconsideration (if any), and an accurate notice of the presently available remedy. That notice must not purport to exclude constitutional jurisdiction. If the statutory Tribunal is not operational, an agency webpage cannot pretend that it is; equally, an administrative complaints portal should not be presented as a substitute for adjudication.

18.2.4 Create the authoritative instruments register

The operative regime cannot be reconstructed from press releases, unversioned downloads and draft handbooks. PVARA should maintain a single public register containing the Act, saved instruments, Federal Rules, PVARA Regulations, Gazette references, commencement and repeal data, binding standards, non-binding guidance, general directions, consultation drafts, feedback statements, forms and superseded versions. Every item should show its legal basis, status, issuer, approval date, effective date and checksum. Drafts should carry a permanent watermark and cease to appear beside operative instruments without a status distinction.

This is not administrative polish. Publication and version control determine notice, reliance, equality of treatment and the evidence available to a court. As at the cut-off, PVARA’s official consultation page still describes the proposed Virtual Asset Services Regulations and activity handbooks as draft and subject to revision, while the licensing page states that full VASP licensing is “coming soon”.417 The current official regulations page displays the Act, NOC material and ART sandbox documents; it does not establish that the consultation draft has become final law. The register should make that status impossible to misunderstand.

18.2.5 Issue a bounded continuity determination

Section 74 should be applied instrument by instrument. For each Ordinance-era NOC regulation, direction, application, order and institutional act, the responsible authority should record: the pre-Act source; whether the subject survives under the Act; whether the content is inconsistent; the new statutory home; any adaptation required; and the date on which it will be replaced. Where the Act requires consultation, Gazette publication or a different decision-maker, savings cannot be used to evade that requirement.

The determination should preserve customer protection and procedural continuity without declaring an NOC equivalent to a section 19 licence. Section 73 may remove a genuine implementation difficulty within its limited life, but it should not be used to add a regulated class, create a levy, enlarge a penalty, change appellate jurisdiction or rewrite the transition. Those are questions of legislative choice.

18.3 Primary legislative proposals

The primary-law package should be a targeted Virtual Assets (Amendment) Bill accompanied by a clause-by-clause compatibility statement. The objective is not to reopen provisions that can work through lawful administration. It is to repair matters that subordinate legislation cannot safely decide.

18.3.1 Clarify perimeter and regulator interfaces

The Act should preserve its functional service definition but add an express substance-first rule: characterisation under the VAA does not displace the law governing currency, deposits, payment systems, securities, derivatives, collective investment, companies, secured transactions, tax or underlying property. PVARA should classify the virtual-asset service; SBP, SECP and other competent authorities should decide questions Parliament has assigned to them. A joint determination mechanism should resolve mixed cases without allowing silence by one body to become approval by another.418

The amendment should authorise a public perimeter register recording anonymised or publishable determinations, the facts treated as decisive, participating agencies and resulting permissions. It should also state the Pakistan nexus for remote and cross-border offerings: targeted solicitation, local distribution, local-currency access, local establishment, material local customer base or other objectively specified connection. A reverse-solicitation exception, if adopted, must be narrow, evidenced and unavailable where the provider cultivates the Pakistan market.

18.3.2 Complete the issuer lifecycle

Sections 18–23, 30–33, 42–43 and Schedule I do not yet supply an entirely clear route for the person issuing on its own behalf. Parliament should distinguish a principal issuer from a professional third-party issuance service provider and prohibit public offering, admission or targeted distribution without the appropriate approval. The statute should confer express power to require a white paper or equivalent disclosure, identify the legally responsible issuer, control marketing, impose continuing disclosure, require redemption or reserve arrangements where promised, and suspend or withdraw an offering.419

The primary text should state the legal consequences of material misstatement, omission, unauthorised offering and failure to honour redemption. It should identify who may claim, the limitation framework, available compensation or rescission, and the relationship with securities and company law. It should not validate an “asset-referenced”, “stable”, “Shariah-compliant” or “real-world-asset” claim by name alone. Where a token represents title, a security interest or a beneficial interest, the underlying law must recognise and perfect that right.

18.3.3 Make customer-asset protection portable across insolvency

Section 24 already establishes segregation, fiduciary responsibility and exclusion of customer assets from the VASP’s estate. The amendment should make the protective consequences executable across custody chains and insolvency forums. It should address sub-custody, omnibus holdings, shortfalls, reconciliation, tracing, permitted lien or set-off, customer consent, return in specie, valuation where return is impossible, and recognition by liquidators and courts.420

The legislation should authorise a Pakistani-law statutory trust or equivalent proprietary mechanism so ownership, control, priority and return can be proved when a VASP fails. Reuse or encumbrance should require authority, informed consent, activity-specific permission and clear loss allocation.

18.3.4 Repair AML/CFT allocation and the issuer gap

The VAA should identify PVARA’s AML/CFT supervisory role in terms aligned with the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2010 and the lawful designation architecture, without compromising the Financial Monitoring Unit’s protected functions. If the relevant Schedule IV allocation or notification has not been validly made and published, it should be made through the instrument required by the AMLA. The VAA’s reference to “FMLI” should be corrected to the legally intended institution.421

The reporting-entity position of principal issuers and other covered participants should be stated expressly rather than inferred from a VASP definition designed around services to third parties. Parliament should confer power for risk-based treatment of self-hosted addresses, unhosted transfers, privacy-enhancing features and cross-border originator/beneficiary information, while preserving legality, proportionality, data minimisation, confidentiality and effective challenge.

18.3.5 Correct enforcement, penalty and appellate architecture

The amendment should implement the Chapter 16 enforcement chain: a single notice architecture; particularised grounds; access to adverse material subject to lawful protection; opportunity to respond except for justified urgent interim action; time-bounded freezes and restrictions; prompt confirmation; reasons; internal reconsideration where appropriate; and effective independent review. Sections 57, 59, 60 and 62–65 require coordinated redrafting so that prohibited conduct, maximum exposure, review, condonation, stay, appellate route and the relationship with constitutional jurisdiction are intelligible.422

The law should distinguish administrative, civil and criminal routes; prohibit double punishment for the same wrong; and state how settlement affects other proceedings. Digital-evidence and key-custody powers require defined thresholds, records, proportionality, return and remedy. Penalties should not import an unlimited maximum from “any other law”.

18.3.6 Correct public-finance, tax and textual defects

Sections 13–15 and the annual-report provision should be aligned with the Constitution, the Public Finance Management Act 2019, federal accounting, audit and appropriation requirements. The amendment should clarify the legal status, custody, permitted application and reporting of the PVARA Fund; retain Auditor-General and parliamentary visibility; and prevent fees or monetary penalties from becoming an off-budget operational incentive.423

Section 66’s reference to the “Income Tax Act” should be corrected to the Income Tax Ordinance 2001. The correction must not be mistaken for creation of a tax charge. Any digital-asset charging, withholding, reporting, valuation or loss rule belongs in the relevant fiscal legislation enacted under the constitutional allocation of taxing power.424 The Act’s numbering and cross-references should be technically corrected, including the annual-report sequence. Section 70 should be amended only if the transition truly cannot be completed lawfully; section 74 should remain a savings provision, not a permanent substitute for Act-era instruments.

Finally, Parliament should decide—not leave to a handbook—whether and how the Authority’s Shariah advisory function relates to a token or product presented as Shariah-compliant. The statute need not make the regulator a religious certifier. It should prevent misleading claims, identify any recognised approval process and preserve the powers of financial-sector regulators whose laws govern the underlying product.

18.4 Federal Rules, PVARA Regulations, standards and guidance

Delegated legislation should be built as a controlled stack. Each instrument needs an enabling-provision table demonstrating that every obligation, discretion, fee, information demand and consequence remains within the Act. Consultation is a quality control, not a substitute for authority. The official 2026 consultation is therefore a valuable input but, by its own published status, not final law.425

18.4.1 Federal Rules under section 67

Federal Rules should address matters assigned to the Federal Government or requiring government-wide procedural authority. The first Rules package should cover:

  • constitution and procedure of the Appellate Tribunal, to the extent the corrected Act lawfully permits;
  • appointment, terms, conflict management and vacancy handling where the Act leaves prescription to Rules;
  • Fund budgeting, accounts, custody, permitted expenditure, internal control, audit support and reporting;
  • lawful fees and prescribed monetary or procedural matters, without converting a fee into an unauthorised tax;
  • service of notices, authentication of instruments and certified electronic records across government interfaces;
  • the process for policy directions under section 71, including Gazette publication and an operational-autonomy assessment; and
  • any prescribed coordination or reporting matter expressly placed with the Federal Government.

Rules should not reproduce the entire licensing handbook. Nor should they be used to decide matters that the Act assigns to PVARA by Regulation. The responsible Division should publish an enabling-power concordance and obtain legal vetting before approval. Completion means Gazette publication, effective date, accessible consolidated text, forms capable of use and the institutional arrangements required by the Rules—not approval of a file note alone.

18.4.2 PVARA Regulations under section 68

The final Regulations should provide the binding operational rulebook. They should be modular enough to update a custody control without reopening unrelated mining or advisory rules, but integrated enough to avoid contradictory definitions and duplicated sanctions. At minimum, the stack should contain:

  • General/licensing: classification, completeness, fitness, ownership, governance, outsourcing, change, surrender, wind-down and public status;
  • Activity permissions: the Schedule I services and any lawfully added category;
  • Prudential: capital, liquidity, insurance, concentration, stress and recovery calibrated to activity;
  • Customer assets: segregation, records, reconciliation, keys, sub-custody, shortfalls and return;
  • Conduct/disclosure: customer treatment, conflicts, execution, fees, complaints, marketing, listing and continuing disclosure;
  • Market integrity: surveillance, records, confidential information, manipulation, listing conflicts and algorithmic-token controls;
  • AML/CFT and sanctions: risk, CDD, beneficial ownership, monitoring, reporting, sanctions and Travel Rule;
  • Technology/data/resilience: governance, access, change, third parties, incidents, continuity, recovery, evidence and privacy;
  • Regulatory reporting: identifiers, prudential, transaction, asset, incident and complaint data with correction history; and
  • Cross-border: Pakistan nexus, foreign conditions, group supervision, data access, reliance and exit.
  • Section 68 publication correction: amend the Act expressly to require Gazette publication, authentication and a stated commencement rule for Regulations; until then, describe the consequence as contestable rather than universally void;

The final text should state which provisions apply during transition and when new duties commence. It should include proportionate bands but preserve minimum duties. It should identify the source and maximum consequence of non-compliance rather than create a free-standing punitive code. Where a handbook contains a mandatory rule, that rule should migrate into the Regulation or a standard validly incorporated under it.

18.4.3 Standards and technical specifications

Standards are appropriate for matters that require precision and controlled revision: Travel Rule message fields and interoperability; customer-asset reconciliation files; wallet-control evidence; cybersecurity baselines; incident categories; application data dictionaries; regulatory returns; proof-of-reserve methodology if used; algorithmic-token stress scenarios; and audit-log retention. Each binding standard should identify the enabling Regulation, version, effective date, change log, conformance test and exception process.

Technical requirements should be outcome-linked. “Use industry-standard security” is not testable. A useful standard states the protected outcome, minimum control, evidence required, test frequency, severity classification and time to remediate. Where several implementations can achieve the result, the standard should avoid locking the market into a named commercial vendor or a cryptographic method that cannot be revised safely.

18.4.4 Guidance, supervisory statements and forms

Guidance should explain how PVARA interprets and administers the law, give worked examples and disclose supervisory expectations. It should say that it is non-binding, identify the provisions explained and state that a materially different lawful method can be demonstrated. A regulated person should not be sanctioned merely for departing from guidance where it complies with the binding rule and achieves the required outcome.

Forms and portals should collect only information lawfully required. Each field should map to an assessment or reporting purpose; sensitive information should have a retention, access and deletion rule. Portal validation should distinguish a technically accepted upload from a legally complete application. Automated risk scores may support triage but should not become undisclosed decision criteria.

18.4.5 Consultation and commencement controls

Before finalisation, PVARA should publish a disposition table showing material comments, accepted or rejected recommendation, reason, and textual consequence. It should perform an authority review, constitutional-rights review, competition and small-provider impact assessment, privacy and cybersecurity assessment, implementation-cost estimate and regulator-capacity test. If a rule cannot be supervised at commencement, that is a design defect, not a reason to pretend compliance can be inferred.

The final package should use staged commencement. Governance, fitness, customer-asset, AML/CFT, disclosure, incident-notification and records duties should apply first or remain continuously applicable. Requirements dependent on new schemas or systems may commence after published conformance testing. Grandfathering should protect orderly transition, not exempt inherited business indefinitely. PVARA should publish the signed final instruments, Gazette evidence where applicable, a clean text and a redline against the consultation draft.426
